title: Nested Conditionals and Guard Clauses
objectives: Refactor deep nesting with guard clauses
Use early returns to flatten logic

content.title: Nested Conditionals
content.explanation: Conditionals can be placed inside other conditionals. This allows complex decision trees but can lead to deep indentation (arrow code).

content.title: Nested Conditional Example
content.explanation: Three levels of nesting. Hard to follow the logic flow.

content.title: Guard Clauses and Early Returns
content.explanation: Guard clauses check preconditions and return early. This flattens nested code by handling edge cases first, then proceeding with main logic at the top level.
key_points: Main logic stays at left margin

content.title: Refactored with Guard Clauses
content.code: print(can_drive(25, True, False))  # Can drive, needs car
content.explanation: Each check handles one failure case. Main success path at bottom. Much easier to read.

content.title: Trace Nested vs Flat
content.explanation: Both produce same results. Flat version is easier to trace and modify.

content.title: Add Guard Clauses
content.code:
def process_user(user):
    # Add guard clauses for:
    # - user is None
    # - user not active
    # - user has no permissions
    _____
    # Main processing here
    return

blanks.hint: Check failure cases first, return early

questions.question: What is a guard clause?
options: A clause that guards a variable

content.title: Key Takeaways
points: Nested conditionals work but hurt readability
Guard clauses: check failures first, return early

quiz.question: What is the maximum recommended nesting level for conditionals?
quiz.explanation: Beyond 2-3 levels, code becomes hard to read. Use guard clauses to flatten.
